title: Bustard, the plains turkey (kurrbal)

identification.basis: The dictionary's kurrbal is 'plain turkey (native companion)'; 'plains turkey' is the bustard's usual name in the north and 'native companion' the brolga's, and the dictionary has kulbal for the brolga, so kurrbal is taken here as the bustard. The Australian bustard is recorded fifteen times within 30 km of Karma Waters.

summary: **[kurrbal](word:kurrbal)** is the plains turkey, the Australian bustard, the big grey ground bird that strides the open [woodland](entry:woodland) and the grass plains of the north, 'about one metre high', with a wingspan 'around twice that length', and that 'when disturbed, often adopt a cryptic pose with neck erect and bill pointed skywards', then stalks away, runs, and flies 'as a last resort' [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-bustard]. It was the biggest game bird of the north: 'this so-called turkey may be speared, the commonest method, as a general rule, everywhere', Roth wrote, and in the west it was noosed with a grasshopper on a switch or surrounded with fires 'dazed with the smoke and din' [ref:roth1901]. It eats what the flats give, 'shoots, roots, leaves, flowerheads, seeds and fruit of plants, a variety of insects, especially grasshoppers', lizards and mice, and it is 'strongly attracted' to the wild oranges of the *Capparis* bushes, which hunters in the north-west used as a trap [ref:wiki-bustard]. The male's display in the breeding season is 'a conspicuous performance that is accompanied by loud booming', the throat sac let down as 'a swaying skirt'; the female lays one egg on bare ground and sits it alone [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[kurrbal](word:kurrbal)** 'plain turkey (native companion)' [ref:hershberger1982]. The two English names in that gloss belong to two birds: 'plains turkey' is the bustard across northern Australia, 'native companion' is the brolga; since the dictionary has **[kulbal](word:kulbal)** for the brolga, *kurrbal* is read here as the bustard, with the caution that the two words are a letter apart [ref:wiki-bustard] [ref:wiki-brolga]. In English: 'bustard, Australian bustard, plains turkey, wild turkey and native turkey', and 'bush turkey' in central Australia, 'particularly by Aboriginal people, who hunt it' [ref:wiki-bustard]. The [scrub turkey](entry:scrub-turkey), *diwan*, is a different bird altogether [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The bird
sections.body:
'A large ground-dwelling bird that is common in grassland, woodland and open agricultural country across northern Australia and southern New Guinea. It stands at about one metre high, and its wingspan is around twice that length. The species is nomadic, flying to areas when food becomes plentiful'. 'Males are up to 1.2 m tall with a 2.3 m wingspan. The average weight for males is 6.3 kg, with a range of 4.3 to 12.76 kg. The female is quite a bit smaller at 80 cm tall, with a 1.8 m wingspan and an average body mass of 3.2 kg'; the heaviest recorded male was 14.5 kg [ref:wiki-bustard].

'The species is mostly terrestrial and usually seen walking slowly alone or in pairs. When disturbed, Australian bustards often adopt a cryptic pose with neck erect and bill pointed skywards. They may stalk gradually away or run if alarmed, taking flight as a last resort. When leaving the ground they take to the air with heavy beats of the wings.' 'The habits of the bird are usually discreet and shy of disturbance, however, the display of males during the breeding season is a conspicuous performance that is accompanied by loud booming. The male is able to expand a sac at the neck to display their longer feathers as a swaying skirt, with the head held proud and upward facing' [ref:wiki-bustard].

'*Ardeotis australis* does not make any attempt to construct a nest. The clutch size is usually one egg, sometimes two, laid close to a small shrub or bush on unadorned ground ... Incubation of the brood is maintained by the female', who 'will crouch and move away if disturbed' [ref:wiki-bustard].

'The species is strongly attracted to capers, fruit of the plant *Capparis nummularia* ... and this behaviour is exploited by Indigenous peoples who dig pit traps around the bush and wait nearby to capture them. The omnivorous diet includes shoots, roots, leaves, flowerheads, seeds and fruit of plants, a variety of insects, especially grasshoppers', and small reptiles and mammals [ref:wiki-bustard].

**Roth's hunting note, 1901.** 'This so-called turkey may be speared, the commonest method, as a general rule, everywhere. In the Boulia District it is either caught with a grasshopper and noose fixed to the extremity of a long thin switch held by the hunter, who gradually creeps forward unobserved, enveloped in boughs and bushes, or else quietly surrounded in the open. In the latter case numerous fires are simultaneously raised in more or less of the line of a circle right round the group of unsuspecting birds which, dazed with the smoke and din now suddenly evoked, are rushed upon and easily knocked over with boomerangs and nullas' [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Bustard, brolga, emu, scrub turkey
sections.body:
- **Bustard**: grey-brown, heavy-bodied, walks with its head up, stands still with its bill in the air; a boom in the breeding season [ref:wiki-bustard].
- **[Brolga](entry:brolga-and-cranes)** (*kulbal*): taller and thinner, grey with a red head, in pairs at the water, dancing; the 'native companion' [ref:wiki-brolga].
- **Emu**: taller again, shaggy brown, a runner [ref:wiki-emu].
- **[Scrub turkey](entry:scrub-turkey)** (*diwan*): black with a red head and yellow wattle, in the scrub, building a mound [ref:hershberger1982].
- **A bustard in the grass with its neck up** is easy to walk past; look for the pale neck and the slow turn of the head [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A big three-toed track** on a sandy flat, the toes thick and the stride long; no hind toe mark [ref:wiki-bustard].
- **A pale shape standing still** in the grass after a fire or at the edge of a burn, where the grasshoppers are [ref:wiki-bustard] [ref:re-woodland].
- **Booming** at dusk and dawn in the breeding season [ref:wiki-bustard].
- **One blotched olive egg on bare ground** by a bush, and a bird crouching away from it [ref:wiki-bustard].
- **Birds walking the wild-orange bushes** when the fruit is on them [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Where it lives
sections.body: 'Grassland, woodland and open agricultural country': the open [woodland](entry:woodland) and the grassy flats, especially the freshly burnt ground and the green pick after it. It is nomadic, 'flying to areas when food becomes plentiful' [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: The grasshopper bird
sections.body: The bustard follows the grasshoppers and the fruit, which means it follows the fire: the early-dry burns of the [woodland](entry:woodland) and the green pick after them are where the insects are, and the bustard walks the edges of the burn with the kites overhead [ref:wiki-bustard] [ref:wiki-whistling-kite]. It takes lizards and mice too, and is taken, as an egg and a chick, by the [goanna](entry:goanna) and the dingo, and as a bird by the [wedge-tailed eagle](entry:woodland) [ref:wiki-bustard] [ref:wiki-wedgie]. Its one egg a year on bare ground is why it has gone from the settled south and why it needs the open country here to be left open and burnt cool [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Booming and display in the breeding season, the warm months into the storms; the egg on the ground after; the birds on the burns in the early dry and on the wild oranges 'after the first thunder-showers in October' [ref:wiki-bustard] [ref:palmer1883]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **The big game bird**: 'may be speared, the commonest method, as a general rule, everywhere' [ref:roth1901].
- **Noosed** with a grasshopper on a long switch, or **surrounded with fire** and knocked down, in the west [ref:roth1901].
- **Pit-trapped** at the wild-orange bushes in the north-west [ref:wiki-bustard].
- **Eggs**, where found; the bird lays one [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Taking a plains turkey
sections.body:
From Roth's North Queensland note and the western methods he recorded [ref:roth1901] [ref:wiki-bustard]:

1. **Find the birds** walking the flats and burns in the morning and evening; a standing bird with its bill in the air has already seen you [ref:wiki-bustard].
2. **Stalk with cover**: the western hunter crept forward 'enveloped in boughs and bushes'; the bird lets a slow bush come closer than a man [ref:roth1901].
3. **Spear** from as close as the cover allows, with the [woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera); 'the commonest method' [ref:roth1901].
4. **Or noose**: a grasshopper tied as bait at the end of a long thin switch with a slip-noose, offered to the feeding bird [ref:roth1901].
5. **Or the fire ring**: a party lights a circle of fires round a group of birds at once and rushes them in the smoke; this is the plains-country method and a bushfire if done wrong [ref:roth1901].
6. **Cook** in the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) as the camp's big birds were cooked [ref:anderson1996].
7. **Leave the sitting birds**: one egg a year, and the female on it [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc].
- A speared bustard is a heavy bird with hard legs; it kicks.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Native birds, the bustard among them, are protected wildlife in Queensland [ref:qld-nca]. Whether *kurrbal* is this bird or the brolga, Kuku Yalanji speakers can say; the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982]. Each place on this page says who holds the country there.

locations.summary: The plains turkey is a bird of this country. In Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park, downstream, 'in the woodland and grassland area the agile wallaby, northern nailtail wallaby and Australian bustard may be found' [ref:wp-rinyirru]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 164 bustard records, from 1963 to 2026, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann]. **On the upper Hann it is still hunted**: the Court recorded a Possum man's evidence of 'hunting pigs, kangaroos, goanna, porcupine, and plain turkeys' [ref:fca-possum].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: Along the Hann the country is 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark trees with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann]: open woodland with grass under it, the bustard's country. The Kuku Thaypan Elders name nine kinds of country, and one of them is ***Kwern***, the open grassy plains [ref:standley2019]. The Atlas count above covers far more country than the river, so read it as 'common in this country', not as a map [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body:
**Wet, December to March**: the rivers flood and the plains go green; 'during this time animals disperse far and wide as food and water is plentiful' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The bustard is nomadic and moves with the food [ref:wiki-bustard].

**Dry, April to October**: the plains dry out, and 'by October the land is brown and parched' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. This is the burning time. The Kuku Thaypan Elders say 'open grassy plains are important for hunting, maintaining grass resources as food and habitat for a myriad of vertebrate and invertebrate species, importantly macropods, small mammals, birds, and reptiles'. At their cool fires 'the birds of prey feed off grasshoppers flying up out of the grass, small mammals and reptiles fleeing' [ref:standley2019]. The grasshoppers that bring the hawks to a burn are the bustard's food too [ref:wiki-bustard].

sections.heading: How people hunted it here
sections.body: A Possum man of the upper Hann told the Court that plain turkeys are among what he hunts [ref:fca-possum]. No hunting method from the Hann, Laura or Princess Charlotte Bay is published. Roth's note that the bustard 'may be speared, the commonest method, as a general rule, everywhere' is for North Queensland as a whole [ref:roth1901]; see the general sections for it.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the **Possum People's** country, held by the Possum Aboriginal Corporation [ref:fca-possum]. The middle and lower Hann are **Thaypan** country, determined on 2 November 2023 and held by the Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation [ref:fca-thaypan]. Rinyirru's Traditional Owners are the Lama Lama and Kuku Thaypan peoples [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Native title holders may hunt for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: The Hunter-Gatherer Language Database has no Kuku Thaypan word for the bustard. Olkola, to the west, calls it **inh-atawangk**, 'plains turkey', and Guugu Yimidhirr, at Hope Vale, **wungguurrga** [ref:hgdb]. Kuku Thaypan speakers' families may know the word; it is theirs to give.

locations.summary: On the upper Mitchell **[kurrbal](word:kurrbal)** strides the open woodland and the grass flats. It is the biggest bird on [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters), recorded fifteen times within 30 km of the homestead, and the first big bird a visitor sees on the station road [ref:ala-aves].

sections.heading: Where it lives here
sections.body: The open ironbark and bloodwood [woodland](entry:woodland) and the grassy flats of Karma Waters, especially the freshly burnt and the green pick, and the station's paddocks [ref:re-woodland]. Fifteen records within 30 km of the homestead. The emu has one record there, so it is not a bird to expect [ref:ala-aves].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: The wild oranges *Capparis canescens* and *C. lasiantha*, whose fruit draws the bustard, are in the Karma Waters records, and Palmer wrote that they flower and fruit 'after the first thunder-showers in October' [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: The fire-ring method is a grass fire; permits and the station's fire rules apply, and the late dry is not the time [ref:kw-about].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Section 211 hunting rights are recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:wyac2020]. Ask the Traditional Owners and the station before hunting.
